The Himalayan File · Day Three · GEOGRAPHY / DISASTER GOVERNANCE

The mountain is not finished with us

Five hundred and seventy-nine dead. Nearly two thousand missing. A hundred people trapped in a hydropower tunnel. And at the top of the valley, where it all began, two newborn lakes that no instrument on earth is measuring.
BY ANANOMUS · OPEN - NEWS

There is a particular silence in the mountains after a disaster, survivors say — the rivers still roar, but the villages go quiet. In Rasuwa district this week, that silence keeps spreading. By Friday evening the flash floods that tore down the Bhote Koshi had killed 579 people, and the search for nearly 2,000 missing had entered its third day. More than 4,500 have been pulled out alive. Of the 183 Indian tourists reported missing, 85 have been found. Ninety-eight have not. Somewhere inside a hydropower tunnel, rescuers are racing to reach about a hundred people who went to work on Wednesday morning and never came out.

To understand what happened, you have to climb — up past the wrecked border post at Rasuwagadhi, past the dozen broken hydropower stations, up the gorge of the Lhende Khola, to roughly 5,200 metres on the shoulder of Langtang Lirung. A mass of glacier ice and rock had held its grip there for centuries. On Wednesday it let go, fell more than a kilometre, and turned itself into something engineers call a debris flow and survivors call a black wall. It gathered water, boulders and momentum, and it arrived at the villages below without a single instrument having warned anyone — because no instrument was watching that slope. It was not on any list. It was not a glacial lake. It was just a mountain, until it moved.

And here is the detail that turns this story from tragedy into policy: the mountain has already written its sequel. Satellite passes over the avalanche source now show two newly formed lakes — 19.80 and 7.28 hectares by the NDMA’s measure — pooling behind unstable walls of rubble called moraines. A private space-analytics firm in Noida confirmed one independently at just over 20 hectares. How much water do they hold? “We don’t have any estimates,” the NDMA’s Krishna Vatsa said, with the candour of a man describing a locked room from outside. Nepal says the flood risk stays until those lakes are fully drained. Nobody yet knows how, or when.

Sit with the asymmetry for a moment. India’s GLOF mitigation programme — the machinery built after Kedarnath and Chamoli — watches roughly 200 known high-risk glacial lakes. It is careful, funded, serious work. And it was irrelevant on Wednesday, because the killer was not a lake until the moment it became one. Early-warning systems watch what exists; the warming Himalaya keeps creating what doesn’t. The scientists at ICIMOD in Kathmandu have been saying this for years in the polite dialect of reports: the hazard is no longer a list of sites, it is a condition of the whole range — a cascading hazard chain, avalanche becoming dam becoming flood, that crosses three countries faster than their bureaucracies can call each other.

That is the deepest layer of this story: the water ignored every border, and the institutions could not. The trigger sat in Tibet, where India has no telemetry and hydrological data-sharing with China survives on lapsed memoranda. The destruction was Nepal’s. The downstream anxiety belongs to Bihar and UP, where the Gandak — which is what the Trishuli becomes — eventually delivers whatever the mountain sends. Four Tamil Nadu ministers flew to Delhi to coordinate the search for their state’s pilgrims; the External Affairs Minister received 21 rescued from the Kailash Mansarovar route, whose bookings had surged this very year. A shared disaster, as one letter-writer put it, beyond borders and geopolitics — and precisely for that reason, a test of whether governance can be shared too. Until upstream data flows as freely as the river, every valley in the Himalaya is reading tomorrow’s news by candlelight.

Public Health · The Regulator Blinks · GOVERNANCE / HEALTH

Two weeks became one day: the surrender of the star system

The food regulator spent four years defending a ratings system the industry loved. On Friday, staring down a Supreme Court deadline, it filed exactly what it had resisted — red warnings on the front of the packet.
BY ANANOMUS · OPEN - NEWS

Regulators rarely change their minds in public. When they do, the timestamp tells the story. The Supreme Court had given the FSSAI two weeks to state its final position on front-of-pack labelling; Justice J.B. Pardiwala had asked, memorably, whether India intended to remain “underdeveloped” in protecting its children from packaged junk. The two weeks were a courtesy. The regulator used one day of them. On Friday it filed its answer: red pictorial warnings on the front of packs for foods high in added sugar, fat and salt.

To feel the size of that reversal, rewind. Since 2022 the FSSAI had championed the Indian Nutrition Rating — stars, like a hotel review, on a packet of chips. The packaged-food industry could live with stars; research kept showing consumers read them as endorsement, a half-decent grade rather than a caution. The rival model — Chile’s black octagons, Israel’s red labels — treats the label not as information but as a warning shot, and the evidence says it works: purchases of “high-in” drinks fell measurably in Chile within two years. India’s own Economic Survey sided with warnings. The regulator held out anyway — until a Kerala NGO’s petition put the question where industry comfort counts for nothing, before a Bench reading Article 21 (the right to health lives inside the right to life) alongside Article 47, the Directive Principle that makes nutrition a duty of the State.

What happens now is the part worth watching, because this is where such reforms have died before. A proposal is not a notification. The thresholds — how much sugar makes a biscuit “high in sugar” — will be fought over gram by gram; the phase-in timeline will be lobbied into geology if nobody watches. But something structural has shifted: the Court now supervises the rule-making, and a regulator that has conceded the principle in an affidavit cannot easily unconcede it. India carries the world’s largest cohort of children being actively marketed into non-communicable disease — over 60 lakh NCD deaths a year, a quarter of adults pre-diabetic or worse. Friday was the day the label on the packet stopped being the industry’s property. The fine print of victory still has to be written; but the font, at last, will be red.

Photo Focus · THE OTHER EXAMINATION
“The label on the packet stopped being the industry’s property.”Warning labels · Article 47 · the Chile model
Thread of the day: Three stories in this paper are the same story — a court forcing a regulator (FSSAI), a court shaming an employer (ISRO workers, Page 2), a court watching a settlement (IBC, Page 3). The judiciary is doing the executive’s quality control. Ask yourself, as you read: is that a strength of Indian democracy, or a symptom?

Lead · Federal Fault Lines · POLITY

A resignation in Srinagar, a bench in Leh: one province, two verdicts on 2019

On the same Friday, a young MP walked out of Parliament over a promise his party could not keep, and a Himalayan territory finally got a court it could reach. Between those two events lies everything still unsettled about the abrogation.
BY ANANOMUS · OPEN - NEWS

Politics occasionally arranges its own symbolism, and Friday was one of those days. In Srinagar, Aga Ruhullah Mehdi — the MP who has spent two years accusing his own National Conference of going soft on Article 370 — accepted party patriarch Farooq Abdullah’s dare and announced he was leaving: the Lok Sabha, by letter to the Speaker as Article 101 requires, and the party, by a charge designed to wound. The NC’s position on restoring special status, he said, is “no different from the BJP’s”. Several hundred kilometres east, across the Zoji La, Ladakh’s Lieutenant-Governor was welcoming the President’s assent to something his territory has wanted since it was carved out in 2019: a permanent bench of the J&K High Court in Ladakh itself, ending the era when justice sat a mountain range away.

Hold the two images side by side, because together they map the unfinished business of August 2019. The J&K Reorganisation Act redrew the map in a day — one state into two Union Territories, one with a legislature on the Article 239A pattern, one without, run under Article 239. The Supreme Court upheld the abrogation in December 2023 but attached a conscience clause: restore statehood “at the earliest”, hold elections. The elections happened. The statehood has not. And in that gap, politics ferments — Mehdi’s resignation is what it looks like when a constitutional wound is left as an electoral promise too long; every party in the Valley must now position itself against a provision that no longer exists but refuses to die.

Ladakh’s story is the quieter, constructive mirror. A territory of 2.7 lakh people had been petitioning for the ordinary furniture of civic life: a public service commission, protection for land and jobs — the Sixth Schedule demand that filled Leh’s streets two winters ago and remains acknowledged but unanswered — and now, at last, a court. Access to justice sounds like an abstraction until you price a litigant’s journey from Kargil to Srinagar in winter. The lesson the examiner — and the honest citizen — should draw is the same from both halves: reorganisation is an event, but institution-building is a process, and the second, slower thing is where legitimacy is actually won or lost. A published roadmap for J&K’s statehood and a straight answer on Ladakh’s Sixth Schedule would do more for the map of 2019 than any anniversary speech.

Labour · The Court Remembers · GOVERNANCE

Rockets on bicycles: the Supreme Court’s history lesson for ISRO

BY ANANOMUS · OPEN - NEWS

The most famous photographs in Indian science are of poverty: a rocket nose-cone strapped to a bicycle in 1963, a satellite riding a bullock cart. We display them as badges of how far we’ve come. This week the Supreme Court turned them into an indictment — because the men who pushed those bicycles, or their successors, are still waiting.

Thirty-four daily-wage workers at ISRO’s Liquid Propulsion Systems Centre at Mahendragiri had fought three decades for permanent absorption. Tribunals ruled for them; the orders were answered in 2012 with a “Gang Labourers Scheme” that kept them temporary in all but name. Justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta struck it down, ordered regularisation through sanctioned posts, and reminded the Union that the State’s duty to be a model employer flows from Article 14 itself. In celebrating our scientists, the Bench wrote, we must not overlook everyone else who carried the enterprise — sometimes literally.

Read this beside last week’s nine-judge “clean slate” on the definition of industry and you can see the whole tension in Indian labour law in one frame: codes and definitions may be rewritten, but the constitutional floor — fairness, dignity, the State held to a higher standard than the bazaar — was reaffirmed here at its most humble address. Forcing a worker to litigate for thirty years, the Court said, is itself the injustice. The bicycle reached the Moon. The man who pedalled it deserved better than a scheme.

“The bicycle reached the Moon. The man who pedalled it deserved a sanctioned post.”Article 14 · model employer · regularisation
Examinations · Governance Repair · GOVERNANCE

The task force asks the burned

BY ANANOMUS · OPEN - NEWS

There is an irony worth savouring in a committee on examination reform holding a public consultation — an exam, in effect, where the students finally set the paper. The Nilekani task force, constituted by the Prime Minister after last year’s convulsions, has invited suggestions from students, parents, teachers and institutions, and the grievance file it will receive is thick: paper leaks that voided years of preparation, eight answer-key errors in a single UPSC prelims, opaque normalisation, and 47 NTA officials sacked in one purge. Parliament has already produced the stick — the Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Act, hardened in 2026 to ten-year terms for organised leaks. What the consultation must produce is the redesign: a testing agency with statutory independence rather than a society registered like a neighbourhood club; error audits published after every exam; grievances resolved before the next cycle, not after. And beneath all of it, the question the country keeps deferring — whether one high-stakes morning should decide a life, or whether assessment can be made continuous, modular, humane. A crore of families will read the answer the hard way.

Internal Security · SECURITY

The two-kilogram intruder

BY ANANOMUS · OPEN - NEWS

Every perimeter the CISF guards — airports, nuclear plants, space centres — was designed against a man with a weapon. The intruder of this decade weighs two kilograms, costs less than a phone, and arrives at two hundred feet. The force has now signed an MoU to train its personnel in counter-drone operations: detection, jamming, spoofing, interception. The context is a year in which cheap drones crossed the western border almost nightly, Operation Sindoor rewrote the military’s assumptions, and the Army raised its first dedicated drone battalion. What India still lacks is the connective tissue — a single national counter-UAS doctrine, so that every force is not buying its own jammers and writing its own rulebook. The shield is being assembled piecemeal while the threat scales industrially; that gap, not any single incident, is the story. Watch for indigenous counter-drone manufacturing under iDEX — the defence-innovation pipeline — to become the next big procurement theatre.

Accountability · Who Checks the Builder? · GOVERNANCE

A third eye on the highway

BY ANANOMUS · OPEN - NEWS

A pothole on a new expressway is never just a pothole; it is a certificate someone signed. Rattled by the build quality of its flagship corridors — monsoon cave-ins, collapsing culverts, service roads that dissolve — the Centre is hiring a third-party inspection agency for expressways and national highways, independent of both the contractor and the authority that awarded the contract. The move concedes a quiet truth: self-certification failed, and audits paid for by the audited are worth what you’d expect. The principle being installed is the oldest one in accountability — the verifier must not be paid by the verified — the same logic as statutory auditors and food-testing labs. Two things will decide whether this is reform or ritual: whether the inspector’s reports are made public, and whether a bad report can actually stop a payment under the EPC and HAM contract models. Sunlight, as ever, is the actual technology.

The Small Print · SHORTS WORTH SIXTY SECONDS EACH

The coaching row sharpens: Jairam Ramesh calls the Centre’s new free online coaching an “accountability-evading gimmick” — the barb lands because a parliamentary panel found the existing free-coaching scheme enrolled just 26% of its target in three years. Scheme announcements are free; outcomes are audited. Keep both numbers together.

A memoir becomes a test case: Congress alleges Penguin India demanded changes in Sonia Gandhi’s memoir under “pressure”; the publisher replies it never held the rights. Beneath the he-said-she-said sits a real question — the quiet narrowing of publishing freedom by anticipated offence. Unverified in parts; watch before citing.

The roll-cleaning pattern spreads: The Hindu’s editorial “Unkind cuts” extends the voter-deletion critique from last week’s Karnataka numbers to Telangana — mass deletions, bulk Form-7 objections, and the old rule from Lal Babu Hussein (1995) that no name leaves the roll without notice and hearing. A one-state story has become a pattern; patterns are what examiners — and courts — act on.

Kerala convoy incident: a probe opens after protesters stopped the Chief Minister’s convoy in Thiruvananthapuram — the eternal boundary dispute between the right to protest and public order, in miniature. MPSC leak mechanics: a 7th-rank holder reveals leaked-paper candidates were told to deliberately wrong ten answers to dodge detection — remember this when someone says leaks are victimless.

Parliament · The Empty Chamber · POLITY

Fifteen percent: the session that barely happened

BY ANANOMUS · OPEN - NEWS

Here is a number to hold against every speech about democracy: in the Monsoon Session just ended, the Lok Sabha functioned for 15% of its scheduled time — among the worst figures in two decades by PRS Legislative Research’s count; the Rajya Sabha managed a third. And yet Bills passed, several in minutes, without debate, in a chamber of shouting and walkouts. Committee referral — the quiet room where laws are actually improved — has become the exception rather than the rule. The arithmetic should bother you more than the theatre: a law debated for four minutes binds a citizen for forty years. Parliament’s deliberative function — the reason the institution exists — is turning ceremonial, and every hour of disruption transfers power from the legislature that shouts to the executive that drafts. When productivity falls this low, the question is no longer who disrupted whom. It is whether anyone still expects the House to deliberate at all — and what an anti-defection-disciplined, whip-run chamber even means when its floor time evaporates.

India Abroad · The Geneva Mirror · IR / SOCIAL JUSTICE

The committee India talked back to

BY ANANOMUS · OPEN - NEWS

In Geneva this week, India sat through its periodic review before UNCERD — the UN committee that monitors the racial-discrimination convention India ratified in 1968 — and heard findings it rejected outright: concerns over hate speech and discrimination flagged against Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and refugees. The delegation called them unfounded; the diplomatic word was “rejected”.

The episode is a compact lesson in how treaty-body review actually works: committees can question, publish and embarrass, but not enforce — sovereignty ends the conversation whenever a state wishes. Yet the mirror matters. India’s own machinery — Articles 15, 17 and 46, the SC/ST Act, the NCSC and NCST — makes the same promises the convention does, which means every rejection abroad is implicitly a claim that the machinery at home is working. That claim, not the committee’s report, is the thing worth examining. International scrutiny is easiest to dismiss when domestic scrutiny is strongest; the order matters.

Medicine · One Nation, One Licence · GOVERNANCE / HEALTH

A doctor’s degree stops at the state line. That may finally end

BY ANANOMUS · OPEN - NEWS

An oddity of Indian federalism: a surgeon licensed in Chennai must re-register, with paperwork and fees, to practise in Hyderabad — as if appendixes differed by state. The National Medical Commission has proposed ending this: one registration with any State Medical Council, one Unique Identification number in the National Medical Register, and the right to practise anywhere in India.

It reads like housekeeping until you count what it unlocks. India’s doctor-population ratio hovers near the WHO floor, but the deeper problem is distribution — physicians pooled in southern metros while the heartland and the Northeast run empty. Portability lowers one real wall to movement; telemedicine, which never respected state lines anyway, gets a legal spine. State councils will resist — registration fees fund them, and public health is a State subject — so watch this as a small, clean test of a recurring Indian question: how much friction between states is federalism, and how much is just rent?

Read this page again, backwards: a Parliament that will not sit, a treaty body India will not hear, a court doing the employer’s conscience for it, a task force asking exam victims to redesign the exam. Every story on this page is an institution being examined by somebody it did not choose — and that discomfort, not any single fact, is what the page is teaching. Institutions that welcome examination pass it; institutions that reject it schedule a harder one. Hold the pattern; the facts will attach themselves to it.

Lead · The Price of a Strait · ECONOMY / ENERGY SECURITY

₹3.89: the journey of a price rise, from a minefield to your fare meter

This morning, a Delhi auto driver pays more for gas because a strait 2,500 kilometres away is mined. Trace the rupee backwards and you hold the entire architecture of India’s energy vulnerability in your hand.
BY ANANOMUS · OPEN - NEWS

Start at the end of the supply chain, at first light: an autorickshaw pulls into an IGL station and the driver discovers his fuel costs ₹3.89 more per kilogram than it did at midnight. He will do the arithmetic all Indian gig workers do — how many extra trips absorb this — and then he will forget about it, because he has no choice. Our job is to not forget, and to run the chain backwards instead. IGL raised prices because the LNG it imports stays stubbornly dear. LNG is dear because the war in West Asia has re-escalated, and every tanker approaching the Strait of Hormuz — the 34-kilometre throat through which a fifth of the world’s oil and LNG must pass — now pays a fear surcharge: insurance, freight, risk. Iran and Oman are negotiating a “joint temporary navigational corridor” through mined water. Until minesweepers finish that sentence, the premium flows downstream — tanker to terminal to pipeline to pump to fare — and lands, as such premiums always land, on the man least able to hedge it.

This is what energy import dependence means when it stops being a phrase in the Economic Survey. India buys over 85% of its crude and roughly half its natural gas abroad. And the exposed nerve is precisely the fuel we chose for our cleanest ambitions: city gas distribution — the CNG fleets and piped kitchens that were the great clean-air bet of the last decade — prices its input off spot LNG markets, which panic faster than crude. The cleaner the city’s fuel mix, the more directly a distant minefield sets its auto fares. There is a genuine irony there, and irony in an economy is usually the sign of an unfinished policy.

Unfinished how? Domestic gas output has idled for a decade despite the HELP regime and open acreage licensing. The gas trading hub, IGX, still trades too thin to discover an Indian price. And the boring, decisive instrument — strategic gas storage, the buffer with which Japan and Korea turn panics into inconveniences — barely exists here; we built petroleum reserves and stopped, as if history had promised our next crisis would be oil-shaped. The fixes write themselves: long-term LNG contracts over spot roulette, storage treated as seriously as the SPR, and SATAT’s biogas quietly blended in as the rural hedge nobody photographs. The next strait crisis is a certainty. Whether it retails at the pump again — that part is a choice, and this morning’s ₹3.89 is the receipt for not yet having made it.

History of Reform · ECONOMY / ESSAY

The decade India lost before 1991: Chidambaram’s beautiful counterfactual

BY ANANOMUS · OPEN - NEWS

The most interesting interview of the week was about a road not taken. P. Chidambaram, looking back at 1991, offered a date that should sting: the reforms, he said, could have begun in 1981. The warning lights were already blinking then — a balance-of-payments squeeze, an IMF loan (the largest in the Fund’s history at the time) — and India took the money, steadied itself, and put structural reform back in the drawer. The crisis passed. The lesson didn’t stick. Ten years later it returned with compound interest: gold flown to London as collateral, reserves worth a fortnight of imports, and liberalisation arriving not as a choice but as an ultimatum.

The counterfactual is worth carrying around because it reframes 1991 from an event into a delayed decision — and delay, in economics, is never free. The decade India spent defending the licence raj is roughly the decade in which East Asia pulled irreversibly ahead; the per-capita gap with South Korea widened most in exactly that window. Chidambaram’s second remark completes the thought: reform could not have come in the era of C. Rajagopalachari — whose Swatantra Party had made the free-market case since 1959 and coined “licence-permit raj” itself. Ideas usually arrive a generation before the State is desperate enough to use them. That is the whole tragedy and the whole mechanism of Indian reform, in one sentence: we act at the point of crisis, and price the delay as if it were prudence. Every “way forward” paragraph you will ever write is an argument against that habit.

“Reform delayed is not reform denied — it is reform made expensive.”1981 IMF loan · 1991 · Swatantra Party
Insolvency · The Credibility Test · ECONOMY

Three paise in the rupee: the haircut that shaves the Code itself

BY ANANOMUS · OPEN - NEWS

Some numbers need no adjectives. Subhash Chandra, founder of the Zee empire, stood personally liable for ₹22,006.57 crore in guarantees to lenders — among them the largest banks in the country. Under a settlement blessed within the insolvency process, he will pay ₹6.5 crore. Do the division and you get three paise in every hundred rupees: a 99.97% haircut, absorbed by institutions that hold your deposits, described even in sober wire copy as “highly controversial”.

The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code was built in 2016 on a single behavioural insight: promoters must believe they can lose everything, or credit discipline is theatre. That is why Section 29A bars defaulters from buying back their own companies cheap, and why the Supreme Court, in Lalit Kumar Jain (2021), confirmed that personal guarantees follow the promoter home. A settlement like this files down the Code’s sharpest tooth in public view — every stressed promoter in India now possesses a template and a precedent. Recovery rates were already sliding, from around 43% in the early years toward the low thirties; haircuts above 90% no longer surprise anyone, which is itself the scandal. A law’s deterrent power is an asset, and assets depreciate. This week the IBC’s depreciated visibly — watch whether the committee of creditors that approved this is ever asked to explain itself, because that answer will tell you who the Code now serves.

Public Health · The Unsolved Outbreak · HEALTH / SCI-TECH

The virus that leaves no fingerprints

BY ANANOMUS · OPEN - NEWS

In the mud-house villages of Gujarat, an old killer is having its worst season in years, and the unnerving part is not the toll — it is the silence in the laboratory. The Chandipura virus, first isolated in a Maharashtra village of that name in 1965, has killed 28 people since early July, almost all children under fifteen. It announces itself as ordinary fever and can end, within 24 to 48 hours, as fatal brain inflammation — acute encephalitis syndrome. Two of every three confirmed cases this season have died, a case-fatality ratio that puts it among the deadliest pathogens in circulation anywhere.

Here is the mystery: the textbook says the carrier is the sandfly, breeding in the crevices of mud walls. But the National Joint Outbreak Response Team has tested more than a thousand samples — sandflies, mosquitoes, ticks, now cattle blood and milk — across this outbreak and 2024’s, and found no trace of the virus in any vector. India is spraying against an enemy it cannot place. The honest name for this is a neglected tropical disease: six decades of recurring outbreaks, no vaccine, no antiviral, no pharmaceutical interest, because its victims are poor children in monsoon districts. The outbreak footprint is quietly widening — Rajasthan, MP, Odisha — and a warming, wetter climate is the suspected hand behind the curtain. A country that eliminated polio can map a virus’s reservoir; what has been missing is not capacity but priority. Twenty-eight small funerals should be enough to reorder it.

The Ledger · MARKETS & POLICY, BRISKLY

Also in the money pages

BY ANANOMUS · OPEN - NEWS

S&P holds India at BBB, stable — growth momentum and the fiscal glide path cited. Ratings move like glaciers; treat the hold as evidence of credibility, not an event.

UPI at ten faces its adulthood question: zero MDR built the network, but fraud control and uptime are not free. A small fee on large merchants — never on users — is the compromise taking shape. The deeper principle: free at the point of use is not free to provide.

Wheat-sugar watch, week two: raw-sugar bookings under the 10-lakh-tonne TRQ import window have begun; mandi wheat firmed after the export ban lifted. The test remains whether export windows become rule-based — announced triggers, not midnight notifications. Predictability is the cheapest subsidy a government can give a farmer.

Aircraft leasing de-risked: the Centre moves on the Cape Town Convention framework so lessors can repossess aircraft without decade-long litigation — cheaper leases, cheaper fares, and a boost for GIFT City’s leasing hub. Dry legal plumbing; real money.

Industrial Policy · The Next Bet · ECONOMY

₹62,500 crore for a phone that is Indian all the way down

BY ANANOMUS · OPEN - NEWS

India assembles the world’s phones; the government has now wagered heavily that it can own them too. The newly notified Mobile Phone Manufacturing Scheme — ₹62,500 crore over five years from 2026-27 — is the PLI idea grown teeth. Its first window rewards scale, as before. The second is the interesting one: reserved for an “Indian brand”, defined with unusual precision — incorporated in India, intellectual property held here, management control and majority shareholding Indian, in-house R&D. Extra incentive flows for domestic sourcing of components; the ministry speaks of sixty thousand direct jobs and cumulative production near ₹39 lakh crore.

The concept underneath is domestic value addition — the gap between assembling and owning. The first PLI round taught India that exports can boom while value capture stays thin: screwdriver work, imported innards. This scheme is the correction, and its fate will answer the industrial-policy question of the decade — whether subsidy can conjure not just factories but brands, the thing Korea and China built and India, so far, has not. Watch the sourcing percentages, not the launch events.

Agriculture · The Sky Relents · ECONOMY / GEOGRAPHY

The monsoon’s late apology

BY ANANOMUS · OPEN - NEWS

June was frightening: the southwest monsoon arrived broken, and with it the oldest fear in the Indian economy. Then July and August repaired what June had ruined — the deficit narrowed, kharif sowing closed to within touching distance of normal, and the RBI’s bulletin exhaled: food-inflation risk easing, rural demand steadying into the festive season.

Two lessons ride on that recovery. First, the monsoon’s intra-seasonal distribution now matters more than its total — the same millimetres, arriving wrongly, ruin a season; an early deficit repaired in July saves it. Second, the margin for error is closing as warming loads the dice toward exactly this kind of lurching, stop-start rainfall. Roughly half of India’s farmland is still rain-fed; the sky remains the finance minister nobody appointed. Every irrigation, micro-irrigation and crop-diversification scheme is, at bottom, an attempt to fire it.

Energy · The Stockyard Problem · ECONOMY / INFRASTRUCTURE

Plenty of coal, none where it’s needed

BY ANANOMUS · OPEN - NEWS

India mines more coal than ever, yet every hot week a fresh set of thermal plants reports critically low stocks. The villain is not geology but logistics: air-conditioning demand keeps smashing evening peaks, and the railway rakes that haul coal from pithead to plant cannot keep pace. Records at the mine, empty yards at the boiler — ambition bottlenecked by freight scheduling.

The forward-looking part: peak demand is now a cooling story, growing faster than any other use of electricity, which means the grid’s future is evening storage — batteries, pumped hydro — and demand management, not merely more baseload. A country that electrified its villages must now learn to survive its own air-conditioners. The coal in the ground was never the constraint; the system that moves and stores energy is.

Lead · The Land COP · ENVIRONMENT / IR

On the steppe where the desert is winning, the world finally wrote a cheque

For twelve days, the diplomats of 196 countries argued about dirt in a city that watches the Gobi advance toward it. They went home yesterday having created something the land conventions never had: money with a mandate.
BY ANANOMUS · OPEN - NEWS

Mongolia was never a neutral venue. Its horsemen cross pastures that thin each year; its winters — the killing dzud — starve herds by the million; official surveys say 77% of its territory is degrading as the Gobi creeps toward the capital. So when COP17 of the UN Convention to Combat Desertification opened in Ulaanbaatar under the banner “Restore land, Restore hope”, the host’s message carried the bluntness of lived experience: the world has enough declarations about land. What it lacks is money and machinery.

Twelve days later, the summit closed having produced some of both — and for the poorest of the three Rio Conventions, the one without the glamour of climate or the charisma of biodiversity, that is nearly historic. The headline is DRIF, the first global finance instrument dedicated to drought resilience; alongside it, $1.3 billion advanced for land restoration with rangelands at the centre, and the Ulaanbaatar Declaration, in which thirty-odd mayors and governors demanded a permanent seat for cities in a convention that has always spoken only to nation-states. The arithmetic stays brutal — pledges cover one billion hectares of restoration by 2030 against up to two billion degraded, and the finance gap is estimated at $278 billion — but a convention that spent three decades adopting language has finally acquired a bank account. Land degradation already touches 40% of the world’s land and 3.2 billion people; drought stalks 1.8 billion. This is not a boutique issue. It is the ground floor of food security.

India should read the Ulaanbaatar file with particular attention, and not only because roughly 30% of its own land is degraded. India hosted COP14 in 2019, pledged 26 million hectares of restoration by 2030, and signed up to Land Degradation Neutrality — yet its grasslands remain the least loved ecosystem in its law, routinely filed as “wasteland” and given away first for every solar park and factory. The UN’s designation of 2026 as the International Year of Rangelands and Pastoralists — a Mongolian initiative — lands differently in a country whose Banni buffalo herders and Deccan shepherds have never had a national policy to their name. The convergence waiting to be built is obvious: restoration finance flowing through MGNREGA’s existing labour architecture, pastoralism treated as a land-management skill rather than an anachronism, and the desertification convention treated as what it actually is — the Rio treaty where India’s food security, employment and climate adaptation all sit at one table, waiting for someone to notice they are the same conversation.

Summit Diplomacy · INTERNATIONAL RELATIONS

Wheels up for Tashkent: a weekend of sitting at difficult tables

BY ANANOMUS · OPEN - NEWS

The aircraft leaves this morning, and the itinerary is a thesis on strategic autonomy. Two days in Tashkent first — Uzbekistan wants Indian investment beyond its pharmaceutical and IT toeholds; India wants uranium, rare earths and a Central Asian partner beholden to neither Moscow nor Beijing. Then on to Kyrgyzstan, where the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation convenes and the seating chart is the story: India at one table with China, Russia, Pakistan and Iran — a week after the boundary talks in Beijing spoke of an “early harvest” on LAC delimitation, a fortnight before a reported Xi visit to Delhi, and squarely in the teeth of American tariff pressure over Russian oil.

Watch three things. Whether the communiqué’s terrorism language is something India can sign without wincing — it has refused dilutions before. Whether Chabahar and the INSTC are named out loud, because Central Asia access runs through Iran or it does not run at all; the port and corridor are the only physical answer India has to Pakistan’s veto on land transit. And whether a Modi–Xi pull-aside moves the boundary file. The SCO is frequently dismissed as a talking shop, which misses the point: for India it is a hedge platform — Eurasia’s table, held simultaneously with the Quad’s, without apology to either. Holding contradictory tables is not confusion. This weekend, it is the doctrine itself, airborne.

Margin notes from a hot world: Syria’s new president appoints Kurdish commander Mazloum Abdi presidential adviser days after his forces dissolved into the national army, and Kurdish-language schooling is authorised — a once-in-a-generation experiment in minority integration, unfolding at the Euphrates’ edge. And in the Strait of Hormuz, Iran–Oman minesweeping talks inch forward; Page 3 told you what their pace costs a Delhi auto driver each morning.
The Long Game · CULTURE & CHARACTER

Sixty-four squares, one first

The boy who learned chess because his sister needed a practice partner has become the first Indian to win the Grand Chess Tour, beating Fabiano Caruana in the final. Use him precisely, because the story is bigger than him: Viswanathan Anand opened this door alone in the 1990s and held it open for a generation; today India fields the world champion (Gukesh, at eighteen), Pragg, Arjun Erigaisi, Vaishali — not a miracle but a pipeline: academies, state federations, the great democratisation of online chess. That is the line worth keeping for any essay on institutions: one genius is luck; a pipeline is policy. Nations that mistake the first for the second keep waiting for lightning. Nations that build the second get weather.

The Week’s Throughline · SYNTHESIS

Institutions that watch, mountains that move

Hold this week in one hand. A mountain created two lakes faster than any register could list them. A food regulator produced in one day, under a judge’s stare, what it had resisted for four years. A promoter settled a ₹22,006-crore obligation for ₹6.5 crore inside a law written to prevent exactly that. A virus killed twenty-eight children while a thousand lab samples came back clean. And the desertification convention, after thirty years of declarations, finally opened a bank account.

Different pages, one pattern: institutional latency — the lag between the moment reality changes and the moment institutions notice. Early-warning registers, labelling rules, insolvency deterrence, disease surveillance, climate finance: all were built for a slower world, and everything you read in this paper today was some part of the system straining to catch up. Keep the formulation; it will serve you in an essay, an interview, an argument: modern governance is a race between the speed of events and the speed of institutions — and every reform is an attempt to shorten the lag. Twenty-eight words. The whole newspaper is inside them.

The Back Page Ledger · HOUSEKEEPING

What we left out, and why

An honest paper shows its cutting-room floor. We dropped the IPO listings and index moves (no durable concept beneath the froth), the Maharashtra Marathi-for-drivers order (state politics until a court makes it a rights question), the TMC hoarding scuffle in Kolkata (heat, no light), and the celebrity-adjacent noise that clogs every feed on a Saturday. The Penguin–memoir affair earned only a short because its facts are still contested — a rule worth internalising: never build an argument on a story still being reported.

Sources, cross-checked: The Hindu Morning Digest and sci-tech desk (new glacial lakes; NDMA), Indian Express legal desk (ISRO judgment) and Ahmedabad bureau (Chandipura), UNCCD official releases and Down To Earth (COP17), PIB (schemes), TOI wires (GLOF panel, third-party inspections), Shankar IAS and Vision IAS dailies as the coaching-layer check. Where sources disagreed, the primary document won. Where nothing primary existed, we said so or stayed silent — the discipline this paper owes you every single morning.

The Map Room · FIVE PLACES THIS PAPER VISITED — FIND EACH ONE ON AN ATLAS TONIGHT

Rasuwagadhi, the broken border post where this week’s grief began, sits on the Nepal–Tibet crossing north of Kathmandu; the Trishuli that drowned it becomes the Gandak in the plains and meets the Ganga at Hajipur, opposite Patna. One river, three names, two countries’ anxieties.

Ulaanbaatar, where the land convention finally found its money, is the world’s coldest capital, ringed by degrading steppe between the Altai and the Gobi — a city whose winter smog and summer dust are the same story told in two seasons.

The Strait of Hormuz, which set a Delhi auto fare this morning, bends between Iran and Oman’s Musandam peninsula; its shipping lanes run three kilometres wide each way. A fifth of the world’s oil moves through a corridor narrower than many city bypasses.

Tashkent, today’s destination, is Central Asia’s largest city — an old Silk Road junction where an Indian Prime Minister, Lal Bahadur Shastri, died in 1966 the night after signing a peace. History keeps its appointments there. And Mahendragiri, where ISRO’s engines are tested and its daily-wagers finally won, waits in Tamil Nadu’s Tirunelveli district under the last great massif of the Western Ghats.

The last word, for the walk to the tea stall: a river changed its name three times on the way to the Ganga and carried a tragedy across a border; a desert convention learned to write cheques; a chess player made a pipeline look like a person. If a single sentence survives from this edition, let it be this — geography is the syllabus the earth sets, and institutions are how humans answer it. Every page you read today was one species of that answer: fast where the water came, slow where the paperwork lived, and — on one Saturday in August — occasionally, unexpectedly, just.
